title: To contemplate and hand on (ST II-II.188.6)
hookLine: better to light others than only to shine

cards: A friend finishes a book that changed something in them, and for a week your phone keeps buzzing. A photo of a page. A line underlined twice.
"You have to read this." Whatever lit them up, they can't keep it to themselves.
Thomas Aquinas asked a question that sounds dry and isn't: which is the better life, one spent quietly gazing at God, or one spent busy doing good? His answer was neither, exactly.

teach.b: The question sits near the end of the long second part of the Summa, where Thomas weighs different ways of religious life. Some communities mostly pray, in silence. Some mostly serve: nursing, feeding, building.

Thomas says contemplation, looking at God in prayer, is the higher thing in itself. But he puts a third kind of life highest of all: contemplating, and then handing on to others what you've seen. Teaching.
Preaching. His picture is a lamp. It's a greater thing to give light than only to shine.

A lamp glowing in an empty room is lovely; a lamp that lets someone find the door does more. The Latin phrase that comes out of this article is contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on to others what you've contemplated.
Tradition says Thomas's own order, the Dominicans, took it as a motto.

Notice the order: first you look, then you give. Thomas isn't praising busy people who never stop to pray, or people who only talk. The handing on has to come out of real looking, or there's nothing to hand on.
Elsewhere in the Summa he points to the life of Jesus himself, who taught out of his own prayer.

teach.h: TO LIGHT, NOT ONLY TO SHINE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works."
One honest note: this is Thomas's argument, and the Church holds all these callings dear.

teach.h: SO LET YOUR LIGHT SHINE BEFORE MEN.
teach.b: Enclosed nuns who pray for the world, and sisters who run a hospital, aren't failing a test. Thomas is describing the shape of a gift: what you receive in silence grows when it's given away.

how: Dominicans describe their life with the phrase contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on what has been contemplated, and Catholics draw on Thomas's article when they speak about prayer feeding teaching and preaching.

games.q: what does “to contemplate and hand on” mean?
o: looking at God, then giving others what you saw
a quiet life of prayer kept wholly to oneself
staying busy with good works instead of prayer

games.q: to contemplate and hand on — tap the pairs.
p: so let your light shine before men

s: Thomas says busy good works matter more than prayer
he calls contemplation the higher thing in itself. what he puts highest is contemplating and then handing it on.
Thomas's image is that giving light is greater than only shining
a lamp that lights the room does more than one that only glows.
for Thomas, praying communities are failing a test
the Church holds all these callings dear. Thomas is describing the shape of a gift, not failing anyone.

games.q: you're Thomas, asked which life is best: quiet prayer, or active good works. what do you answer?
o: active works, because they help people.
contemplating, then handing on what you've seen.
quiet prayer alone, never speaking of it.
games.why: Thomas puts highest the life that contemplates and then hands it on: better to light others than only to shine.

practice: Look back over what you've learned lately, from this path, a book, a hard week, someone older, and let one thing rise that actually helped you: not the cleverest thing, the truest.
Hold it a moment, the way Thomas would, just looking at it, then picture one person who could use it. If you pray, ask for the right moment to pass it on.

wordCard.voice: To contemplate and hand on. For Thomas, a life that looks at God and then gives others what it has seen, a lamp that lights the room, not only itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: to hand on to others the things contemplated.

carryVoice: Your line: light others. A lamp does the most when someone finds the door by it. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works
